title: Why Are My Allergies Worse Indoors?
h1: Why Are Your Allergies Worse Indoors? Common Triggers and Fixes
description: Allergies worse at home? Dust mites, pet dander, mold and dirty ducts or filters are common culprits. Here's how to find the trigger and clean up your air.
quick_answer: Allergies often feel worse indoors because allergens like dust mites, pet dander, mold spores and pollen get trapped inside and keep circulating. Closed windows, a low-grade or dirty HVAC filter, dusty ductwork and damp spots all make it worse. Better filtration, humidity control and regular cleaning usually bring noticeable relief.
body:
It feels backwards. You come inside to get away from pollen, and the sneezing gets worse. The reason is simple: your home holds onto allergens. Whatever comes in, or grows inside, tends to stay there and keep circulating every time the heating or AC runs.

This article covers the common triggers and the practical fixes. If your symptoms are severe or getting worse, talk to your doctor or an allergist, since they can test for the specific things you react to.

What are the most common indoor allergy triggers?

Dust mites

Dust mites are tiny creatures that live in bedding, mattresses, upholstered furniture and carpet. They like warmth and humidity, which is one reason coastal homes can have a harder time with them. It's their waste particles, not the mites themselves, that trigger reactions.

Pet dander

Cats and dogs shed tiny flakes of skin that float in the air and settle into carpet, couches and ductwork. Dander is light and sticky, so it hangs around long after the pet has left the room.

Mold spores

Mold grows where there's moisture: bathrooms without good exhaust fans, under sinks, around leaky windows and in damp crawl spaces. It can also grow inside an AC system if the drain pan or coil stays wet. Spores travel through the house easily.

Pollen that came inside

Pollen rides in on clothes, shoes, hair and pets, and through open doors and windows. During Santa Ana wind events, outdoor dust and pollen can get pushed in through every small gap in the house.

Smoke and fine particles

Wildfire smoke, cooking smoke and fireplace use all add fine particles that irritate the nose, throat and lungs. They're not allergens in the strict sense, but they can make allergy symptoms feel a lot worse.

How does your HVAC system play a part?

Your heating and cooling system moves the air in your whole house, so it can either help clean it or spread allergens around. A few things make a big difference:

  • The filter. A thin, cheap filter catches big dust but lets fine allergens pass. A clogged filter restricts airflow and stops doing its job.
  • The ductwork. Years of dust, dander and debris settle inside ducts. Leaky return ducts in the attic or garage can also pull in insulation fibers and dust.
  • Moisture at the coil. A slow drain or dirty coil can grow mold that gets blown into the house.

If you notice symptoms flare up when the system kicks on, or you see dust blowing from the vents, the system is worth checking.

How can you reduce indoor allergens?

You don't need to do everything at once. Start with the simple steps and work up:

  1. Upgrade and change your filter. Use a pleated filter rated for fine particles that your system can handle, and replace it on schedule. Ask a technician if you're unsure which rating fits your equipment.
  2. Wash bedding weekly in hot water. Allergen-proof covers on mattresses and pillows help too.
  3. Vacuum with a HEPA vacuum. Regular vacuums can blow fine dust back into the air.
  4. Keep pets out of the bedroom. It gives you at least one room with less dander.
  5. Control humidity. Run bathroom and kitchen exhaust fans and fix leaks quickly. Coastal homes may benefit from a dehumidifier.
  6. Close up during high-pollen days and wind events. Keep windows shut and let the filtered HVAC system do the work.
  7. Take shoes off at the door. It keeps a surprising amount of outdoor dirt and pollen off the floors.

When should you call a professional?

If you've done the basics and still feel worse at home than anywhere else, the problem may be in the system itself. Our indoor air quality services can help with:

  • Upgraded media filters or whole-home air purifiers that work with your existing system
  • UV lights that help keep the cooling coil and drain pan free of mold growth
  • Whole-home dehumidifiers for damp coastal homes
  • Air duct cleaning and sealing when ducts are dusty, leaky or contaminated

A technician can inspect your filter setup, coil, drain and ducts and tell you which of these would actually help your home, rather than selling you everything at once.
faqs: Why are my allergies worse at night?

Your bedroom is where dust mites concentrate, in the mattress, pillows and bedding. Lying down for hours puts your face right next to them. Weekly hot washes, allergen covers and keeping pets out of the bedroom usually help.
Can dirty air ducts make allergies worse?

They can. Dust, dander and debris collect in ducts over time, and leaky ducts can pull in dust from the attic or garage. If you see dust blowing from vents or symptoms flare when the system runs, have the ducts inspected.
Does an air purifier help with indoor allergies?

A good purifier can reduce airborne particles like dander, pollen and smoke. Portable units help in one room, while whole-home options work through your HVAC system. Neither replaces regular cleaning and humidity control.
How often should I change my HVAC filter for allergies?
Check it monthly and change it whenever it looks dirty, especially if you have pets or during smoke and windy seasons. The right schedule depends on the filter type and how often your system runs.
